newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: New PCW desirable but not at any price - Irish SFA.
newsitem.headline: New PCW desirable but not at any price - Irish SFA.

text.p: A new Irish social partnership arrangement is desirable but not at any price, the Small Firms Association (SFA) said on Thursday as it urged the government to keep tighter control on the public finances.
The current agreement between government, unions and employers, the Programme for Competitiveness and Work (PCW), expires at the end of 1996 and is due for renegotiation shortly.

The SFA said the PCW and its two predecessors had helped bring about significant benefits to almost all sections of Irish society but these benefits could have been greater and could have been better distributed.
It said in a report on social partnership that in each of the last six years, increases in Irish government expenditure have been higher than inflation.
One of the largest increases in current public expenditure had been the payment of public sector employees, it said.

If public sector pay increases over the period from 1987 to 1995 has been held in line with inflation, there would have been over one billion punts available in 1995 alone for substantial tax cuts, the SFA said.
"In reality, the hard won and very rare opportunity for tax cuts and job creation has been discarded for the increased living standards of public sector employees."

It called for a new form of social partnership over the period 1997-1999 under which the quantitative targets to receive the greatest focus would not be wage guidelines but strict controls over public finances.
It said there must be no further significant increases in public sector pay and special pay increases should be abolished and the public and private sector pay deals made consistent.
The SFA said a major structural reform of the public finances should take place with the budgetary process replaced by multi-annual accounting.
It recommended that the government set itself binding targets for the public finances -- 69 percent for the debt/GNP ratio and 30 percent for the tax/GNP ratio -- to be achieved by 1999.
